new_statements.quote: Stress in Engdewu is not phonemic. Primary stress normally falls on the penultimate syllable, or on the ultimate syllable if this is heavy, i.e. containing a long vowel or a coda. Secondary stress normally falls on every second syllable to the left of the primary stressed syllable. [...] Notice that heavy syllables attract stress and may change the stress pattern. [...] Loudness and vowel length are the major features of stressed syllables in Engdewu. [...] The pitch on the other hand is relatively flat throughout the word, and plays a minor role in stress assignment. [...] Note that the stress rules in Engdewu have not been investigated in detail, and there may be patterns that deviate from what has been said here.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Non-contrastive word stress: primary stress on the penultimate syllable by default, shifting to the final syllable when that syllable is heavy (long vowel or coda consonant); i.e. a right-aligned moraic trochee (Vaa explicitly likens it to Lynch's 2000 POc analysis). Could equally be coded weight-sensitive (final if heavy, else penult); most words end in open light syllables so the surface pattern is 'mostly penult'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on every second syllable to the left of the primary-stressed syllable (e.g. [ˌjɞŋiˈbaŋgɒ] 'we felt (it)'; [ˈnig tʉˈkɒːlɒˌpⁿme] shows heavy syllables perturbing the pattern).
new_statements.exceptions: Heavy final syllables (long vowel or coda) take primary stress ([iˈβɵm] 's/he came' vs [ˈiβɵ] 's/he went'); heavy syllables generally 'attract stress and may change the stress pattern'; closed syllables are increasing among younger speakers (final unstressed /u/ whispered by elders, elided by the young, yielding final codas); emphatic lengthening of a stressed vowel; author's caveat that stress rules were not investigated in detail. Sec. 4.3 notes Wurm's 1969 transcriptions put stress on the penult in 21 of 32 long-vowel items, the mismatches being numeral (verbal) forms with final long stressed vowels (e.g. tʉˈliː 'two').
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress, illustrated on citation forms and inflected verb/pronoun words, with a spectrogram (Fig. 4.14) of /nidabwe/ [ninˈdambwe]; acoustic correlates intensity + duration, flat pitch. Vowel length only marginally phonemic, and Vaa reanalyses many of Wurm's long vowels as stress-induced lengthening.
new_statements.identity_note: Vaa 2013 describes Engdewu (the speakers' own name; = Nanggu/Nagu of Wurm and Ethnologue, ISO ngr, glottocode nang1262), spoken in three villages on the south coast of Nendö (Santa Cruz), Temotu Province; same languoid as the target, no dialect split described. Wurm 1969/1970 'Nanggu' is the same language (his sec. 3.2.6 / 3.5).

readall_conflicts: The listed work could not be opened, so nothing new was read. The catalog's existing statement (Vaa 2013, sec. 4.7.1, pp.125-126: stress not phonemic; penultimate, or final if heavy; secondary stress on every second syllable leftward) stands. One mild tension exists with Wurm's published note derived from the SAW2 fieldwork (Wurm 1969 p.63, already held by the project): Wurm found only some of the stress pattern predictable and thought stress 'may be phonemic', whereas Vaa 2013 states stress is not phonemic and gives a weight-sensitive rule while conceding (p.126) that 'the stress rules in Engdewu have not been investigated in detail, and there may be patterns that deviate from what has been said here.' Wurm's remark is a hedge from preliminary 1960s notes, not a competing placement rule, so it does not overturn the catalog reading.

sources.note: Ch.4 Phonology, sec. 4.7.1 Stress (pp.125-126): stress not phonemic; primary stress on the penult, or on the final syllable if heavy (long vowel or coda); secondary stress on every second syllable leftward; correlates are loudness and vowel length, pitch flat; compares to Lynch (2000) POc right-to-left moraic trochees; caveat that stress rules not investigated in detail. Ch.4 intro (p.69): 'Stress is mostly penult.' p.119: 'Word stress is basically penult in Engdewu'. Sec. 4.3 discusses Wurm (1969) length/stress transcriptions of 147 items.
